question.problem:
What is the first term that exceeds $1\,200\,000$ in the following geometric sequence?

$$
3,\,3\sqrt{6},\,18,\,18\sqrt{6},\,…
$$
question.worked_solution:
The first term of the sequence is ${a}_{1}=3$ and the common ratio is

$$
r=\frac{3\sqrt{6}}{3}=\sqrt{6}.
$$

So, the $n$th term of the sequence can be written as:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & ={a}_{1}\cdot {r}^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot (\sqrt{6})^{n-1} \\  & =3\cdot {6}^{(n-1)/2}\end{aligned}
$$

We want the $n$th term to be greater than $1\,200\,000.$
Hence:

$$
\begin{aligned}{a}_{n} & >1\,200\,000 \\ 3\cdot {6}^{(n-1)/2} & >1\,200\,000 \\ {6}^{(n-1)/2} & >400\,000 \\ \operatorname{log}⁡({6}^{(n-1)/2}) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(400\,000) \\ \frac{(n-1)}{2}\cdot \operatorname{log}⁡(6) & >\operatorname{log}⁡(400\,000) \\ \frac{(n-1)}{2} & >\frac{\operatorname{log}⁡(400\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(6)} \\ n-1 & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(400\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(6)} \\ n & >\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(400\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(6)}+1\end{aligned}
$$

Estimating the right-hand side using a calculator, we get:

$$
\frac{2\operatorname{log}⁡(400\,000)}{\operatorname{log}⁡(6)}+1≈15.398
$$

Therefore, the $16$th term is the first term of the sequence that exceeds $1\,200\,000.$
